The severity read without the forgiveness is a caricature of the Lord, and the forgiveness read without the severity is a softening that the sūrah did not make. The sūrah holds the two in the same breath, and the holding is the faith the sūrah asks for: the acceptance of the Lord as the one who is severe and loving at once, and the acceptance of the sūrah's law as the expression of both.

**Mercy Inside the Sūrah of Fire**

The sūrah is known for the pit and the curse, and the sūrah itself sees to it that it is known for the names of the mercy. The two names sit at the center of the description of the Lord, between the severity and the sovereignty, and their position is the position of the hinge. The sūrah's fire was real, and the sūrah's curse was real, and the names of the mercy are real in the same measure, and none of the three cancels the others. The structure of the sūrah says that the image of the Lord that survives the sūrah is the whole image, not the image of the grip alone. A reader who meets the sūrah only through the pit meets a fragment, and the sūrah's own arrangement provides the correction: the fragment of the grip stands inside the chain that ends in the love. The two names are the sūrah's answer to the temptation to read the sūrah only as a sūrah of wrath, and the answer is structural: the names are placed where the structure gives them weight, at the center of the description, where they hold the severity and the sovereignty together. The sūrah of the fire is, by its own structure, also the sūrah of the All-Loving, and the two names together are the sūrah's last word about the one before whom the case of the pit was heard.
verses.15:
> Lord of the Throne, the All-Glorious

**The Seat of the Sovereignty**

The chain of the description moves from the character to the seat: the Lord of the Throne. The attribute places the sovereignty announced in the ninth verse on its seat, and the seat is the Throne, the greatest of the things that exist, the throne of the one who owns the heavens and the earth. The sūrah that began by measuring the king of the ditch against the kingdom of the heavens and the earth now names the Lord by the throne, and the measurement is complete. The king of Najrān had a court and a fire and a crowd, and the Lord named here has the Throne, and the distance between the two seats is the distance the sūrah has been stating since the ninth verse. The attribute is the sūrah's answer to the tyranny of the pit, given in the form of a name rather than an argument, and the name carries the whole argument inside it. The attribute also completes the sūrah's answer to the question of power. The sūrah began by asking, in the form of the oath, by what power the verdict stands, and the oath answered with the sky, the Day, and the witness. The description of the Lord answers the same question from the Lord's side: the power is the sovereignty, and the sovereignty has a seat.

**The Throne and Its Bearers**

The Book describes the Throne with its bearers, and the bearers are the angels. "Those ˹angels˺ who carry the Throne and those around it glorify the praises of their Lord, have faith in Him, and seek forgiveness for the believers" (40:7). "On that Day eight ˹mighty angels˺ will bear the Throne of your Lord above them" (69:17). The image the sūrah's verses assemble is completed by these: the Lord is borne, carried by the mightiest of the creation, and the bearing is the standing state of the sovereignty. The sūrah's own imagery of the sitting — the persecutors who sat around the pit — is answered here by the imagery of the bearing. The two images face each other across the sūrah: the ones who sat are the ones who are judged, and the one who is borne is the one who judges. The sūrah's picture of the court of the pit and the Book's picture of the court of the Lord are the two halves of the sūrah's argument, and the attribute in this verse names the second half.

**A Scale the Name Carries**

The Book sets the scale of the Throne against the heavens and the earth, and the scale is stated in the verse of the testimony: "His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest" (2:255). The Seat, the Kursī, is the thing that encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the Throne stands above the Seat, greater than the thing that already encompasses all. The two words of the sūrah — Lord of the Throne — carry that whole scale without naming it, because the name of the Lord by the Throne is the name that contains the scale. The sūrah does not need to state the magnitude; it needs only to name the seat, and the seat does the stating. The king of the pit measured his power by the length of his roads, and the Lord measures His by the Throne, and the difference between the two measures is the difference the sūrah exists to make.

**The Grammar of the Glorious**

The second word of the verse carries a grammatical ambiguity that the exegetes record, and the ambiguity is a gift rather than a defect. The word al-Karīm, the All-Glorious, can be read in the nominative case, in which it describes the Lord: the Lord of the Throne, and He is the All-Glorious. It can be read in the genitive case, in which it describes the Throne: the Lord of the Glorious Throne. The two readings agree on the point that matters: the glory belongs to the seat and to the one who holds it, and the verse says both at once. The grammar of the Arabic allows the one word to carry the two descriptions, and the sūrah's use of the word is the use that takes the allowance. The glory is not an ornament added to the sovereignty; it is the sovereignty's own quality, the quality that the seat has and the Lord has, and the verse names the quality in the case where the two are joined.

**The Throne Against the Fire-Pit**

The chain of the description of the Lord rises from the grip to the throne, from the severity to the sovereignty, and the rising is the sūrah's final movement about its judge. The five verses of the description — the grip, the origination and the return, the forgiveness and the love, the throne and the glory, and the will that is done — form a complete picture of the one before whom the case of the pit was heard. The king who built the pit is measured against the Lord of the Throne, and the measurement is the sūrah's last word about the two. The image of the throne is the sūrah's last image of the judge, and it is the image that carries the whole argument of the sūrah in a single noun. The sūrah's description of the Lord ends here, and the sūrah turns to a new unit, the question about the other destroyed forces, and the turn marks the end of this block. The throne is the sūrah's highest image of the judge, and the image stands where the sūrah has placed it: at the end of the description, after the severity and the mercy, as the seat that holds both.
verses.16:
> Doer of whatever He wills

**The Attribute That Signs the Block**

The chain of the description ends with the execution of the will: He does whatever He wills. The attribute closes the block the way a signature closes a document, and what it signs is everything the block has stated. The grip of the twelfth verse was not the last word about the power of the Lord; the last word is that the will of the Lord is done, without impediment, without delay, without exception. The sūrah closes its description of the God the way it opened its case against the pit: with the certainty of the outcome. The makers of the ditch were certain in their own way, certain that the fire would make the believers change, and the sūrah's answer is a certainty of a different order, the certainty of the will that does what it wills. The two certainties are not equal, and the verse states the difference by naming the one that ends all the others.

**The Book's Standing Formula**

The formula is the Book's standing one, used at the moments when the argument is ended. "Surely Allah does what He wills" (22:18). "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between. He creates whatever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything" (5:17). The sūrah's verse stands in the family of these, and the family's function is the same in each case: to end the question. The verses of the family are not used to begin an argument but to close it, and the sūrah's use of the formula at the end of the description of the Lord follows the family's standing practice. The argument of the sūrah — the argument that the pit was a crime, that the crime is judged, that the judge is the Lord of the Throne — is ended by the formula, and the ending is the sūrah's statement that no counter-argument stands inside the will that is done.

**The Will and the Case**

For the sūrah's case, the execution of the will is the guarantee that the verdict stands. The curse of the fourth verse is not a wish, and the sentence of the tenth is not a threat in the human sense of the word; both are entries in the record of the will that is done. The arrangement the persecutors made — the ditch, the fuel, the crowd, the ultimatum — was an arrangement inside the will, and the arrangement could not stand against the will it was inside. The sūrah's verse states the relation: whatever the Lord wills is done, and the will includes the verdict on the makers of the ditch. The persecutors' power was real as far as it went, and it went no further than the will allowed, and the sūrah's closing attribute states the limit of their power and the ground of the verdict in the same words. The case of the pit is closed by the will, and the closing is final in the sense the sūrah means by final. The verse also states the limit of the persecutors' project. The project was to make belief disappear by force, and the force was real as far as the force of the pit went. The sūrah's answer is that the project was inside a will larger than the pit, and the will is done. The disappearance of belief by force was never an event that could stand; it was an attempt inside the will, and the attempt ended where the will placed it.

**The Block Complete**

The five verses of the description of the Lord form a complete block, and the block is the sūrah's second movement. The pivot to the God in the ninth verse; the two verdicts in the tenth and the eleventh; and the five attributes in the twelfth through the sixteenth, the grip, the origination and the return, the forgiveness and the love, the throne and the glory, the execution of the will. The block describes the Lord from the power to the character to the seat to the will, and the sequence is the sequence of a complete statement. After the block, the sūrah turns to a new unit, the question addressed to the Prophet about the story of the other destroyed forces, and the turn is the mark that the block is finished. The sūrah has judged the pit, balanced the scale between the two fates, and described the judge, and the description ends where the sūrah's argument needed it to end: at the will that does what it wills.

**The Middle of the Sūrah**

Read together, the verses from the ninth to the sixteenth form the middle of the sūrah, the movement that carries the sūrah from the historical case to the standing law and from the standing law to the description of the judge. The case of the pit is the sūrah's occasion, but the law and the description are the sūrah's substance, and the substance is what survives the occasion. The sūrah has now done everything the sūrah of the pit needed to do: it has condemned the makers of the ditch, it has sentenced the persecutors who do not repent, it has promised the believers their gardens, and it has stated the power, the character, the seat, and the will of the one who judged. What remains in the sūrah is the reminder that the same judgment has fallen before on the mighty forces of the past, and the statement of the standing of the Book itself in which the judgment is recorded. The middle of the sūrah is where the sūrah becomes more than its occasion, and the block from the ninth to the sixteenth is the proof of the claim. The block ends, and the sūrah's next unit begins with a question.
verses.17:
> Has the story of the ˹destroyed˺ forces reached you ˹O Prophet˺—

**The Question That Opens the Third Movement**

The sūrah leaves the description of the Lord and turns to a question addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: has the story of the forces reached you? The opening of the sūrah's third and final unit is a question addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and the turn is the sūrah's last change of direction. The first unit carried the oath and the case of the pit; the second unit carried the verdicts and the description of the Lord; and this unit carries the reminder, the reminder that the case of the pit is one instance of a standing pattern. The question is the hinge between the particular and the general, and the sūrah places it exactly where the particular ends and the general begins. The Book addresses its Prophet in the second person at its moments of reminder, and the address is not a report to be passed on but a reminder to be received, so that the one who carries the sūrah is the first to be reminded by it.

**The Word for the Forces**

The sūrah names its examples by the word for the forces, the armies, the gathered might of a people. The Arabic, ʿasfar, carries the sense of the organized strength, the power arrayed for the action, and the word does the selection of the examples. The sūrah does not say "has the story of Pharaoh and the story of Thamūd reached you" as two separate tales; it says "the forces," and the word gathers the two under the single name of the organized might. The choice of the word is the sūrah's first statement about the two stories: what is at issue in both is not a man or a tribe but the might, the gathered power of the people arrayed against the truth. The forces are what the sūrah is about, and the forces are what the sūrah's verdicts of the previous unit have already judged. The question asks the listener to hold the two stories under one name, and the name is the name of the power that is destroyed. The word also does the sūrah's quiet work of comparison. The force of the pit in the first unit was the organized might of a town with its ditch and its fuel, and the forces named in this unit are the armies of the river and the tribe of the valley. The word holds the two scales together, and the sūrah's argument moves from the smaller force to the larger without changing the name.

**A Story Everyone Had Heard**

The form of the question is the form of a shared memory. Has it reached you, the sūrah asks, as if the story might not have, and the form is the form of a check rather than a report. The stories of the two named forces were known in the world the sūrah addressed: the story of the Egyptian king and his army was the standing tale of the prophets' books, and the story of the Arabian tribe and its rocks was the tale of the region, the tale that the people of the region told of the carved houses and the broken camel. The sūrah does not tell either story in this verse; it summons both from the listener's memory, and the summoning is the point. A reminder that tells its tale from the beginning is a report, and a reminder that summons the tale already known is a warning, and the sūrah's unit is the warning. It is the call to the memory, and the memory is the evidence the sūrah brings without repeating it.

**The Two Examples, Chosen**

The sūrah will name the two forces in the next verse, and the choice of the two is the choice of the sūrah's argument. The two together cover the world the listener knew and the world beyond it: one name was the foreign king, the ruler of the river and the sea, and the other was the Arabian tribe, the people of the valley and the rock. The sūrah does not choose two examples of the same kind; it chooses one of each kind, so that the pattern it is stating holds in every corner of the listener's world. The selection says that the fate of the forces is not the fate of a region or a dynasty but the fate of the forces, wherever they are gathered and whatever their shape. The two names are the two ends of the range of the power, and the sūrah's unit will state the fate that is common to the two ends. The choice also says what the sūrah's first unit did not need to say: the case of the pit was not a local event. The local event was the instance of the pattern, and the pattern is stated here in the two names that cover the world.

**The Structure of the Sūrah**

The sūrah has now completed its arrangement, and the question is the mark of the arrangement's final unit. The opening oaths and the case of the pit occupied the first block; the verdicts and the description of the Lord occupied the second; and the question, the answer in two names, the statement of the denial, the statement of the encompassing, and the two verses of the Book occupy the last. The unit of the question is the sūrah's reminder, and the reminder is what the sūrah leaves with its listener after the case and the verdicts have been stated. The sūrah could have ended at the description of the Lord, and it does not, because the sūrah's purpose is not the case but the standing of the pattern, and the pattern is stated in the unit that begins with this question. The sūrah's last act of address is the question, and the answer it receives in the next verse is the two names that the whole unit turns on.
verses.18:
> ˹the forces of˺ Pharaoh and Thamûd

**Two Names for Every Kind of Power**

The answer to the question is two names, and the two names are the sūrah's whole argument in its compressed form. The sūrah does not answer with a narrative; it answers with the two designations of the two destroyed forces, and the designations carry the narratives inside them. The first name is the name the world knew for the king of the river: Pharaoh, the ruler of the army that met the sea. The second is the name the region knew for the tribe of the valley: Thamūd, the people of the carved rocks. The two names together are the sūrah's range: the power of the water and the power of the rock, the foreign dynasty and the Arabian tribe, the army of the plain and the settled people of the hollow. The sūrah's choice of the two is the selection of the argument, and the argument is that the fate of the forces is one fate, whatever the kind of the force.

**The Army That Met the Sea**

The first name carries the story the listener already holds. The Book tells the story of the king and his army in several of its sūrahs, and the telling is constant in its shape: the signs shown, the denial, the pursuit, and the sea. "And We certainly showed Pharaoh all of Our signs, but he denied them and refused ˹to believe˺" (20:56). The pursuit that followed is the story's end: "But as Pharaoh was drowning, he cried out, 'I believe that there is no god except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am ˹now˺ one of those who submit'" (10:90). "Then We drowned the others" (26:66). The army that had pursued across the land met the water, and the water took the king and the soldiers together. The sūrah's first name is the name of that end, and the sūrah does not need to retell the story, because the name is the end. The force of the river, the gathered might of the plain, the king who arrayed the army, all of it stands under the one name, and the name stands at the place where the sea closed.

**The People of the Rocks**

The second name carries the story of the region. Thamūd were the people of the valley, the tribe that carved its houses into the rock of the stone hollow, the people of the carved homes that the sūrah of the dawn will name again: "and Thamûd who carved ˹their homes into˺ the rocks in the ˹Stone˺ Valley" (89:9). The Book tells their story in its own shape: the messenger sent to them, the sign set before them, the refusal, and the taking. "And He destroyed the first ˹people of˺ ʿĀd, and ˹then˺ Thamûd, sparing no one" (53:50–51). The destruction that took them is told in the sūrah of the Overwhelming: "which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees" (69:7). The tribe's story is the story of the sign and the refusal. The sign was the she-camel of the Lord sent to them as the proof of the messenger: "A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is Allah's she-camel as a sign to you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah's land and do not harm her" (7:73). The refusal made the sign an act: "Then they killed the she-camel —defying their Lord's command— and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, 'Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers'" (7:77). The force of the rock, the settled might of the hollow, the tribe that had carved the mountain, all of it stands under the one name, and the name stands at the place where the wind passed and the houses stood empty.

**Why the Sūrah Pairs Them**

The pairing is the sūrah's selection of its case. The sūrah could have chosen any two of the destroyed peoples the Book names, and it chooses these two, and the choice is the argument. The first is the power that moved, the army that pursued across the land and met the water; the second is the power that stood, the tribe that carved the rock and met the wind. One end of the range is motion and the other is station, one is the gathered host and the other the settled town, one is the might of the river and the other the might of the mountain. The sūrah's statement, made through the pairing, is that the fate is the same at the two ends. The pairing is also the sūrah's answer to the objection that the first name might draw: the objection would be that the king of the river is a power of another land, far from the listener, and the answer is the second name, the power of the listener's own land, whose houses the region still saw standing empty. The force that moved was taken, and the force that stood was taken, and the taking is the taking of the forces, not of the men who led them. The sūrah's unit will state the fate in the next verses, and the pairing is the premise of the statement.

**The Question and Its Answer**

The unit of the sūrah is a question and two names, and the form is the form of the reminder rather than of the report. The question in the previous verse asked whether the story had reached the listener, and the answer is the two names, because the names are the story for the one who knows it. The sūrah does not repeat the tale of the sea or the tale of the wind, and the non-repetition is the sūrah's confidence in the memory it is addressing. A sūrah that retells its examples from the beginning treats the listener as one who has not heard, and a sūrah that names its examples treats the listener as one who has heard and must now be reminded of what the hearing means. The sūrah's listener is the second kind, and the two names are the reminder's whole content: the forces were these, and the forces were destroyed, and the sūrah's next verses state what the destruction means for the ones who hear it and still deny.
verses.19:
> Yet the disbelievers ˹still˺ persist in denial

**The Rejection of the Reminder**

The two names are the reminder, and the verse states the response to the reminder: the disbelievers persist in denial. The sūrah has done the work of the reminder completely. It has told the case of the pit, it has named the two destroyed forces, and it has placed the two names before the listener as the standing pattern. The verse does not add to the reminder; it records the reception of the reminder, and the reception is the denial. The form of the verse is a statement of fact about the disbelievers, not a repetition of the argument, and the form says that the argument is done. The sūrah will not argue with the denial; the sūrah has argued, and the argument stands, and the denial is now a fact of the case rather than an objection to it. The verse is the sūrah's record of the failure of the reminder to work as a reminder, and the record is the sūrah's quietest statement about its listener. The verse is also the sūrah's record of its own limit. The sūrah can give the evidence, and it can state the response, and it cannot take the response away. The taking is the work of the encompassing in the next verse, and the sūrah knows the division of its own labor.

**The Word of the Denial**

The verb of the verse is the word for the denial, the refusal, the saying-no to what is shown. The Arabic, yankirūn, is the present form, and the present form states the habit rather than the act: the disbelievers are not denying one sign at one moment; they are in the state of the denial, the state that the sūrah's own grammar named at the pit. The persecutors of the pit were in the state of the witnessing, shuhūd, and the disbelievers of the reminder are in the state of the denial, inkār, and the sūrah's grammar of the standing state runs through the two units. The denial is not a position they hold; it is the condition they are in, and the condition is what the verse states. The state-form of the verb is the sūrah's way of saying that the denial is not a moment of weakness but a settled posture, and the settled posture is what the sūrah's verdicts of the previous unit were addressed to.

**The Denial of the First**

The word of the denial is the word the Book uses of the first of the two named forces. The king of the river met the signs in the same state: "And We certainly showed Pharaoh all of Our signs, but he denied them and refused ˹to believe˺" (20:56). The signs were shown, and the denial was the response, and the response of the present disbelievers is the same response in the same word. The sūrah's verse does not make the connection explicitly; it makes it by the word. The denial of the present is named with the name of the denial of Pharaoh, and the naming is the sūrah's statement that the present is the same case as the first. The two names of the previous verse were the two forces, and this verse gives the two forces their common name, the name of the state that met the signs in both of them. The inheritance is stated in a verb, and the verb is the word the Book already used at the river.

**A Choice, Not an Ignorance**

The verse's first word does the work of the whole statement: yet. The sūrah has given the evidence, and yet the denial, and the particle states the relation between the two. The denial is not the absence of the evidence; the evidence is present, the case is told, the names are given, and the denial stands in front of the evidence. The verse assigns the cause of the denial to the one who denies, and the assignment is the sūrah's diagnosis. The denial is the choice against the shown, not the ignorance of the shown, and the choice is what the sūrah's law of the previous unit punished. The statute of the tenth verse punished the persecutors who did not repent, and the denial of this verse is the state that keeps the persecutors on the side of the punishment: the denial is the refusal of the door. The sūrah's logic is complete at this point: the evidence is given, the response is the denial, and the denial is the choice that stands where the door was. The particle yet is the sūrah's way of placing the burden where the burden belongs, and the placement is the verse's quiet judgment.

**The Final Form of the Crime**

The crime of the sūrah began at the pit with the persecution of the believers for their belief, and the crime ends in this verse with the denial of the signs. The two are the same crime in its two forms: the denial is the root, and the persecution is the fruit. The persecutors of the pit were able to build the fire because they had first denied what the fire was built against, and the disbelievers of the reminder continue the denial now that the fire is spent. The verse closes the sūrah's unit of the reminder with the diagnosis of the whole sūrah: the case of the pit was not an accident of a tyrant but the working of the denial, and the denial is the standing state of the one who stands against the shown. The sūrah has now stated the crime in its two forms, and the next verse states the position of the one who denies, which is the position of the encompassed.
verses.20:
> But Allah encompasses them from all sides

**The Answer to the Persistence**

The sūrah answers the denial with a statement of position rather than a counter-argument. The disbelievers persist in denying, and the sūrah's response is not another sign, not another name, not another form of the reminder; the response is the fact that surrounds the denial: Allah encompasses them from all sides. The answer is the sūrah's quietest and its heaviest. It does not argue against the denial; it states the condition of the denier, and the condition is the encompassing. The denial is an act, and the encompassing is the place, and the act is inside the place, and the sūrah states the place. The form of the verse is the form of the answer that ends the argument, and the sūrah uses it here because the argument has been made and the denial has been recorded, and what remains is the position of the one who denies inside the reach of the one who denies against.

**The Word of the Encompassing**

The word of the verse is the word for the complete surrounding, the taking-in from every side, the holding of the object inside the circle without a gap. The encompassed has no outside; there is no direction in which the encompassed can move that is not already inside the encompassing. The sūrah's verb states the condition of the disbelievers in the same grammar it used for the persecutors at the pit: they are in the state of the encompassed, the state that the verse states as a fact of their position. The word is the Book's standing word for the relation of the Lord to the creation, and the sūrah's use of it here is the use of the word at its full weight: the disbelievers deny, and the denial does not move them out of the circle, because the circle is not a place they can leave. The encompassing is the condition, and the condition is the answer. The word also carries the sense of the holding, the grip that keeps the object in its place, and the sense connects the encompassing to the grip of the twelfth verse. The grip of the Lord and the encompassing of the Lord are the two faces of the same power, one face acting and the other face holding, and the two units of the sūrah use the two faces.

**The Word That Took the Forces**

The encompassing is the word of the taking, and the taking of the two named forces was the encompassing made visible. The army of the river was encompassed by the water: "Then We drowned the others" (26:66), and the sea closed on the king and the soldiers together. The tribe of the rock was encompassed by the wind that passed: "which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees" (69:7). The encompassing of the two forces was the encompassing that took them, and the encompassing of this verse is the same encompassing in its present form: the circle is already around the disbelievers, and the taking has not yet come because the taking is the closing of the circle that is already drawn. The sūrah's verse states the drawn circle, and the two stories of the previous verse show what the drawn circle becomes.

**The Unseen Encompassing**

The source of the verse is the verse's own point: the encompassing is the state of the unseen. The disbelievers can see the world they move in, and they cannot see the circle, and the inability to see is what they take for the absence. The Book states the relation of the unseen encompassing in its own standing form: "And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺" (2:19), and the secrecy of the deniers is the secrecy that the encompassing holds: "They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people, but they can never hide it from Allah—in Whose presence they plot by night what is displeasing to Him. And Allah is Fully Aware of what they do" (4:108). The encompassing moves with the encompassed, and the secrecy of the denial is inside the encompassing, and the secrecy is the denier's only mistake. The sūrah's verse states the encompassing in its present tense, and the present tense is the sūrah's warning: the circle is now, and the closing is what the circle is for.

**The Sūrah's Last Word on the Deniers**

The sūrah has spoken of the deniers from the first verse to this one, and the encompassing is the last word. The first word was the oath that guaranteed the verdict, and the last word is the encompassing that holds the verdict's subjects, and the two words are the two ends of the sūrah's treatment of the same people. The encompassing is a word of position rather than of event: the event of the taking has not come in the sūrah, but the position of the encompassed is complete, and the position is what the sūrah leaves with its listener. The sūrah does not end on the threat of the taking; it ends on the fact of the surrounding, and the fact is the heavier of the two, because the fact is present and the taking is future. The sūrah's warning sits in the tenses. The encompassing is stated in the present, and the taking of the two forces is stated in the past, and the two tenses together say that the present of the encompassed is the past of the forces waiting to be completed. The sūrah leaves the disbelievers inside the circle, and the circle is the sūrah's last statement about them, and the next unit turns from the deniers to the Book that carries the sūrah's whole case.
verses.21:
> In fact, this is a glorious Quran

**The Particle That Turns the Sūrah**

The verse opens with the particle of the opposition, and the opposition is the sūrah's final act of address. The disbelievers of the previous verse persist in denying, and the sūrah answers the denial with the particle that means "rather" and "no, but": in fact, this is a glorious Quran. The particle does not argue against the denial; it sets the sūrah's own statement against the denial, and the statement it sets against is the identity of what was denied. The denial said no to the reminder, and the sūrah's answer is the name of the reminder: the reminder is not a defeated word; the reminder is the glorious Quran. The particle is the sūrah's last word of the argument, and the argument it ends is the argument of the whole unit: the two forces were destroyed, the deniers persist, the encompassing holds, and the book that states all of it is glorious. The sūrah turns from the deniers to the Book, and the turn is the sūrah's final turn.

**The Word for the Glory**

The word the sūrah gives the Book is the word for the glory, the utmost of the nobility, the magnanimity, the grace. The exegetes take the word to mean the highest of the qualities, the quality that belongs to what is most noble, and they apply it to the Book as a whole rather than to any part of it. The sūrah does not say "these verses are glorious" or "this story is glorious"; it says the Quran is glorious, and the statement is the statement of the carrier rather than of the content. The Book that carries the case of the pit, the law of the persecutors, the promise of the believers, the description of the Lord, and the reminder of the forces is the one thing in the sūrah that the sūrah names with the superlative, and the naming is the sūrah's final word about what it is. The glory is not an attribute added to the Book at the end; the glory is the Book's standing quality, and the sūrah states it where the sūrah's own argument needs the ground of its own authority. The word also carries the sense of the honor that belongs to the bearer, and the sūrah's use of it for the Book is the use of the word for what is honored by the one who honors. The Book is glorious because it is the word of the Lord, and the glory is the standing of the word with its Lord.

**The Other Reading of the Word**

The exegetes record a second reading of the word, and the reading is the reading that takes the glory as the mark of the Book's standing above the creation. On this reading, the glory is the glory of the eternal word, the word that is not made, and the word is given to the Book to distinguish it from the words of the makers. The view is one of the recorded positions, and the sūrah's word carries it without taking sides in the technical dispute that the word entered into later. The sūrah's use of the word is the use of the quality: the Book is glorious, and the glory is what the Book has, whatever the technical account of the glory's ground. The sūrah does not need the dispute; it needs the quality, and the quality is stated in the one word, and the one word is enough for the sūrah's purpose, which is the statement of the Book's standing at the end of the case.

**The Sūrah's Circle**

The sūrah began by swearing by the ordered sky, and it ends by naming the glorious Book, and the two verses are the two ends of the same guarantee. The sky was summoned in the first verse as the order that no one can change, and the Book is named in the last unit as the word that no one will change, and the sūrah's structure places the two at its two ends so that the listener receives the guarantee twice: once in the form of the heavens above, and once in the form of the Book in the hand. The sūrah that opened on the sky closes on the word, and the closing is the sūrah's statement of what remains when the sky's order is taken as the model. The sky does not change its course, and the Book does not change its word, and the two are the two forms of the standing, and the sūrah's circle is closed on the standing. The oath of the first verse was the guarantee of the verdict, and the naming of the last unit is the guarantee of the verdict's carrier, and the two guarantees are the sūrah's bookends.

**The Book That Carries the Case**

The sūrah's whole argument is carried in the Book, and the verse states the carrier at the end of the argument, so that the listener leaves the sūrah holding the name of the one that holds everything. The case of the pit, the law of the persecutors, the promise of the believers, the description of the Lord, the reminder of the forces, and the encompassing of the deniers are all in the Book, and the Book is the one thing in the sūrah that outlasts every other thing in it. The persecutors are judged, the forces are destroyed, the deniers are encompassed, and the Book stands, and the standing is what the sūrah's last unit is about. The verse names the Book as glorious at the point where the sūrah's argument is done, and the naming is the sūrah's final word about its own authority. The next verse states the place where the Book is kept, and the keeping is the other half of the glory.
verses.22:
> ˹recorded˺ in a Preserved Tablet

**The Last Word of the Sūrah**

The sūrah ends not on a threat and not on a promise but on a statement of the Book's keeping. The last word of the sūrah of the fire-pit is the statement that the Book is in the Preserved Tablet, and the statement is the sūrah's final guarantee. The sūrah has spoken of the case, the law, the Lord, the forces, and the deniers, and it closes on the one thing that carries all of it, and the closing is the sūrah's answer to the question of what survives. The persecutors did not survive the case, the forces did not survive the taking, and the deniers do not survive the encompassing, and the Book survives all of it, and the survival is the preservation. The sūrah's last verse is the sūrah's statement of the standing of its own carrier, and the statement is the heaviest word in the sūrah, because it is the word that the sūrah needs in order to stand.

**The Tablet Named**

The name the sūrah gives the Book's place is the Preserved Tablet, and the exegetes record the readings of the name with their grounds. Some take the Tablet and the well-preserved Record named in the sūrah of the Dividing as the one thing: "in a well-preserved Record" (56:78), and the preservation of the two names is the same preservation. Others take the Tablet as the book that is recited near the Lord by the angels, the book that stands above the world of the recitation. Others take it as the Master Record, the Umm al-Kitāb, named in the Book's own verses: "and with Him is the Master Record" (13:39), "And indeed, it is—in the Master Record with Us—highly esteemed, rich in wisdom" (43:4). The readings differ on the description and agree on the standing: the Book is kept at the place above the world, at the place where the keeping is the keeping of the Lord, and the keeping of the Lord is the preservation.

**The Reports of the Tablet**

The tradition carries reports that describe the Tablet, and the reports are the reports of the description rather than the doctrine. It is reported of the Tablet that it is made of the white pearl, and that its height is the distance between the heaven and the earth, and that its width is the distance between the east and the west, and that it is to the right of the Throne of the Lord. The reports are the tradition's way of stating the magnitude of the keeping, and the magnitude is the magnitude of the Lord whose keeping it is. The doctrine of the verse is the preservation, and the description belongs to the report, and the sūrah's word carries the doctrine and leaves the description to the tradition. The reports are recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr, and they state what the tafsīr states: the keeping of the Book is the keeping of the greatest of the things, and the Tablet is the place of the keeping.

**The Preserver of the Book**

The preservation of the Tablet is the work of the Preserver, and the Book states the Preserver in its own standing verse: "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" (15:9). The sūrah's last two verses are the application of the promise: the Quran is glorious (21), and the Quran is in the Preserved Tablet (22), and the one who preserves is the Lord the sūrah described in its middle. The chain of the sūrah closes at this point: the grip, the origination and the return, the forgiveness and the love, the throne and the glory, and the will that is done are the attributes of the one who keeps the Book, and the keeping is the work of the same will that does whatever it wills. The sūrah's description of the Lord and the sūrah's statement of the Book's keeping are the two halves of one statement, and the last verse is the half that names the place.

**Preserved From What**

The preservation is named in the Book's own terms, and the terms are the terms of the guarding against the change. The preservation is the guarding against the increase, the decrease, the distortion, and the change, and the guarding is the standing work of the Preserver. The sūrah's own history is the proof of the verse: the sūrah of the pit has outlasted the pit, the sūrah of the persecutors has outlasted the persecutors, and the sūrah of the forces has outlasted the forces. The Book that carries the case of the persecution stands in the world after the persecutors are gone, and the standing is the preservation made visible in the world of the reader. The preservation is not a doctrine about the text apart from its history; the preservation is the history of the text in the world, and the history is the outlasting. The sūrah's last verse is the statement of the outlasting, and the outlasting is what the sūrah has been since the first verse.

**The Circle Closed on the Keeper**

The sūrah began by swearing by the ordered sky, and it ends by naming the preserved Book, and the two ends are the two forms of the same guarantee. The sky is the order that does not change its course, and the Book is the word that does not change its keeping, and the sūrah's structure places the two at its two ends so that the listener holds both. The sūrah of the fire-pit is the sūrah of the standing: the standing of the verdict on the pit, the standing of the law on the persecutors, the standing of the promise on the believers, and the standing of the Book in the Tablet. The last word of the sūrah is the word of the keeping, and the keeping is the work of the Lord whose attributes the sūrah stated in the middle, and the sūrah's circle is closed on the keeper. The fire was the last word of the persecutors, and the preservation is the last word of the Book, and the two last words are the sūrah's balance, and the balance is the sūrah.
